doc.title: DeFranco Buddy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: The Art Tatum of the clarinet and melting into the instrument
summary: Benny Golson heard his records in Philly; he talks about Tatum, Parker and Shaw becoming one with their instruments.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Yeah, that’s later. I thought it was interesting to read that while you were having all this success and having all these recordings made, that back at home Benny Golson was listening to you and listening to your recordings with Coltrane.
So they’re back in Philly listening to the success story.
And they called you the Art Tatum of the clarinet. That’s a high compliment.
Yeah, which is an exaggeration, but I like that. [laughter]
[laughter] I can imagine, I’d like that, too.
In fact, I wound up doing an album with Art Tatum; great, it was a great experience. You see, there again, scary…
I mean, this guy, because he was a, I still consider Art Tatum and Charlie Parker in the genius area.
I think I, somewhere you described Tatum and Charlie Parker—and I don’t remember who else—as melting into their instrument.
That’s a nice description. Maybe Coltrane and Artie Shaw, I think.
Yeah, their instruments and they become one. I used to try to do that with the clarinet and I was successful, sometimes, you know.
Yeah, I would imagine that would be a great feeling when you accomplish that.
Yeah, when you, when you’re not conscious of plunking your, and…

Working at it. DeFranco:…and working at it. It just, there’s a flow that just happens out of your mind and body. And you become unified with that instrument, so the instrument becomes apart of you. And I watched Artie Shaw, that’s exactly what he portrayed when he played, and of course, Bird and Art Tatum.
